architecture.mechanism: Combustion-induced engine noise can be characterized and isolated from overall engine noise via vibro-acoustic signal processing (vibration, acoustic, in-cylinder pressure) combined with coherent power spectrum analysis and time-frequency methods (Wigner-Ville distribution), which identify the dominant frequency band linked to the combustion process.
architecture.intervention: Mount a triaxial accelerometer on the 2021 Toyota RAV4 engine block and a microphone near the engine bay, record the grinding noise with the vehicle stationary under repeated no-load run conditions, and process the signals using coherent power spectrum analysis followed by Wigner-Ville distribution to determine whether the dominant energy lies in a combustion-related band or in a mechanical/auxiliary band.
architecture.expected_effect: If the grinding noise's spectral energy concentrates in a frequency band coherent with cylinder pressure (combustion-related), the noise source is the combustion process (e.g., abnormal combustion/misfire); if the energy falls outside combustion bands, the source is mechanical (e.g., bearing, accessory drive, water pump, starter/flywheel gear), which is consistent with the absence of a warning light and with battery replacement not resolving the issue.
architecture.falsification_test: Repeat the measurement on a known-good 2021 RAV4 at the same stationary no-load conditions and compare the time-frequency energy distribution; if the grinding-noise spectrum does not share the same dominant frequency band and coherence with in-cylinder pressure as the reference vehicle, the combustion-noise mechanism is falsified and a mechanical source should be investigated instead.

challenge.kill_reason: the mechanism-space distinctness adjudication counts 1 materially distinct mechanism(s) (< 2, mechanism_distinctness/2.0.0) — the run generated nothing worth attacking (Art. LXXXIV, R514)
